speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That review goes beyond the law, beyond the narrow context of sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This particular review here, which I am going to speak about, is on the context of sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Stiff and effective punishments are necessary, but they are only one part of the picture.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The penalties may deter, but they are not going to remove the attitudes behind such conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, for the purposes of my Statement, I will focus specifically on our approach on punishments that sexual and hurt offenders will face.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, in September 2019, we have the case of a 22-year-old university student who molested a woman on a MRT train.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second case was in July 2020, a 22 year-old university student caused hurt to his ex-girlfriend.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He had put his hands around her neck, choking her and pressed her eye as well.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was given a 12-day Short Detention Order (SDO), 80 hours of Community Service Order (CSO) and a five-month Day Reporting Order (DRO).

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The third case in July 2020, a 23-year-old undergraduate, used a handphone recorded a video clip of a female person in a bathroom.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He was sentenced to a 14-day Short Detention Order and a 130-hour Community Service Order.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: AGC felt that the sentence was too light and they appealed, but the sentence was upheld in Court.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There were also other cases where male university students took videos of females in bathrooms.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There was a public sense that the sentences were not adequate, questions were asked – was there more leniency because of the educational qualifications of some of the offenders?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In this speech, I will set out the Government's approach on sentencing adult offenders for hurt or sexual offences; and second, what should be the relevant factors in sentencing.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When it comes to sentencing, the Government decides on the policy, puts it before Parliament and the philosophy, principles – what we want to see in the laws, what should be the range of sentences, what factors are relevant – those are matters of policy that the Executive works on and puts before Parliament and Parliament decides.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Thus, it is for the Government and Parliament to decide whether the punishments are adequate.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Courts look at the laws, the range of sentences and decide each case on its on its facts, because sentencing in the end is fact-specific.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, when it comes to sentencing, what should our philosophy be?

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are four principles that are often referred to.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: First, prevention – where an offender poses a threat to public safety, the sentence should prevent the offender from causing further harm.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Two, deterrence – the sentence should deter the offender as well as others from similar behaviour in future.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Three, rehabilitation – the sentence should, where and to the degree appropriate, seek to encourage the reformation of the offender.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Four, proportionate punishment – the sentence should punish the offender according to his blameworthiness and seriousness of crime.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now deal specifically with sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Government takes a tough approach on sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have made significant amendments over the years to enhance the protection for victims of sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have set them out in the Annex.

speaker: The Minister for Law (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Members may also access these materials through the SG Parl MP mobile app.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If I may carry on while that is being distributed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That would include: victims in intimate and close relationships with the offender; children under the age of 14; domestic workers; and physically or mentally disabled victims who are substantially unable to protect themselves from abuse, neglect or self-neglect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, if you take the unfortunate case for the Myanmarese foreign domestic work Ms Piang – if those facts had taken place after 1 January 2020, then those found guilty could face much higher punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, giving another example, there was a case some years ago, husband and wife abused their foreign domestic helper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The husband had slapped, punched and kicked the victim, hit her with canes and bamboo sticks and pushed her against the cabinet.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The wife had slapped and punched the victim.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They were convicted of numerous offences including voluntarily causing hurt under the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The husband was sentenced to 43 months' imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The wife was sentenced to two months imprisonment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If those assaults had taken place after 1 January 2020, their sentences are quite likely to have been higher because the penalties have been enhanced.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also specifically made criminal acts like voyeurism, dissemination of intimate images without consent – these have become more prevalent with technology – the conduct were offences previously, but not specifically identified as voyeurism offence or a dissemination of intimate images offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Voyeurism, for example, previously would have been charged under insulting a person's modesty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Dissemination of intimate images, for example, would have been charged under distributing pornography.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have also enhanced penalties under POHA for harassment of persons in an intimate relationship with the offender and for repeated breaches of Protection Orders.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In 2018, the CPC and the Evidence Act were amended.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The accused and counsel were required to seek the Court's permission before questions could be asked about a victim's physical appearance, sexual behaviour, where these do not relate to the charge.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also prohibited the release of identity of victims before a complaint is made and the default position for trials is closed-door hearings when the victim testifies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We also allowed the use of physical screens to shield victims from seeing the accused when testifying in court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Earlier in 2012, the Evidence Act was amended to remove provisions based on outmoded assumptions about victims of sexual offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When it comes to sentencing of adult offenders who commit sexual and hurt offences, our position is that the sentences must reflect that such acts are deeply offensive to our fundamental values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Outrage of modesty is not merely an offence that a man commits because he is tempted by the way a lady dresses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Voyeurism is not merely a thoughtless act that a young student commits in a moment of folly.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These and other similar offences, whether committed against a female or male victim, should be dealt with seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These actions must be seen as an affront of fundamental values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There can in general, be no excuses for these offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mitigation pleas based on the offender's educational qualifications or academic potential should not carry much weight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For such offences, principles of proportionate punishment and deterrence should generally take precedence over rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This means, if you touch a woman inappropriately without her consent, if you upload intimate images of an ex-girlfriend or any other woman; if you video record a woman showering, you must face serious consequences in law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you should not be able to come to Court and say you have a bright future you will go far and so on.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can go far, but first serve the sentence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If we make examples of some offenders, however bright their potential outlook in life, then the message of deterrence will likely be stronger.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am going to ask MOE to summarise these points and send to all students, boys and girls, so that everyone understands where we stand, and they must realise that a moment of folly can lead to very serious consequences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will make sure our laws reflect this severity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: An offender, for example, may have a very low IQ, that affected his judgement as to right and wrong; or a serious mental illness that had a causal link to the offending conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Relevant offender-specific mitigating factors should generally continue to be taken into account.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These factors should be assessed on a case-by-case basis with due consideration given to the harm caused to the victim and the need for deterrence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With this in mind, I will set out three steps that we are going to take now: one, increase penalties for three specific sexual offences; two, AGC will generally object to rehabilitative sentences for adult offenders who commit certain sexual and hurt offences; and three, a guide on sentencing will be published.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, increase in penalties for three sexual offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Members know, I have been coming repeatedly to amend these laws and you can see that from Annex 1A.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We did a further review of our penalties for sexual and hurt offences in the Penal Code, including voyeurism, distribution of intimate images, outrage of modesty and voluntarily causing hurt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In our view, the maximum penalties are properly calibrated for most of these offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have set them out in Annex 1B.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are, however, three areas where we intend to increase the maximum punishments.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, outrage of modesty under section 354(1) of the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: From 2016 to 2020, on average, we had 1,190 cases of outrage of modesty reported each year, which is about 24% higher than the previous period of 2011 to 2015.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Next, where sexual activity in the presence of a minor takes place, or sexual images are shown to a minor between the ages of 14 and 16 years; and if you compare that with exploitative sexual activity in the presence of a minor or showing a sexual image to a minor who is between the ages of 16 and 18 years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, unless there are exceptional facts, AGC will, as a general rule, object to rehabilitative sentences for adult offenders who commit certain sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Where adult offenders – I emphasise adult – commit sexual and hurt offences, the need for proportionate punishment and deterrence must take precedence over rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This is a matter for the Government to decide.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I should add that that is the general position they have taken anyway, but they are going to be much stricter about it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will need to give due consideration to exceptional circumstances, which may justify deviation from this general position.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to, in Parliament, and the Executive, and of course, AGC in court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, where the facts of the case are such that rehabilitation should be the dominant sentencing consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take a situation, where a first-time adult offender with an intellectual disability touches a woman.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may, in certain circumstances, better serve the public interest to impose a rehabilitative sentence with appropriate conditions, to reduce the likelihood of future re-offending, rather than to impose an imprisonment term.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Take another example, where the offender suffers from a treatable psychiatric condition that contributed to the commission of the offence, a Mandatory Treatment Order may be appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third step that we will take is to publish a guide on sentencing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To better educate the public about the sentencing process, MHA and MinLaw have worked with AGC and the Law Society and we have prepared a guide on sentencing in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This guide explains sentencing process in our courts, addresses important questions of public interest like: (a) what are the objectives of sentencing?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: (b) what are the common types of sentences imposed by the Courts?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: (c) what factors does the Court take into account during sentencing?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: (d) how does the Court decide what sentence to impose?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The guide will be published on the MHA, MinLaw and AGC websites.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Therefore, if I may summarise this part, in respect of sexual and hurt offences, based on what I have said, it should be clear that an offender will not receive a lighter sentence simply because he has higher educational qualifications, or has better prospects in life.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is another important step that we are going to take.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: MHA and MinLaw have also been considering how we can achieve greater consistency in sentencing and how there can be greater public education about sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We studied the experience in other jurisdictions: England and Wales, and Scotland.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We noted that the formation of a Sentencing Body that promulgates sentencing guidelines can be useful.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can enable proactive publication of guidelines to pre-empt or address areas of concern, and that can facilitate a more consultative process.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it will allow views of more stakeholders to be taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To illustrate, if the Panel decides to issue a sentencing guideline for a hurt-related offence, the Panel can set out the sentencing framework, sentencing bands, based on the twin factors of harm and culpability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The framework can include relevant aggravating and mitigating factors to be considered in sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The guidelines will be published and be accessible to the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be persuasive, but of course, not binding on the Courts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Courts decide each case on the facts before them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We envisage that in working out the guidelines, the Panel will consult other stakeholders, where appropriate.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that will provide greater clarity to the public about the likely sentence and the relevant factors to be considered in sentencing, as compared to the current position where the legislation only sets out the maximum penalties.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is expected to be an inter-agency Panel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will comprise stakeholders from the criminal justice system, including Members of the Judiciary, AGC, MHA and SPF.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We will give more details on the Panel later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The second case, the 22-year-old university student who hurt his ex-girlfriend in May 2019.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The sentence in the case was decided in accordance with the law at the time and rightly so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He would have been liable for up to twice the maximum penalty.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because that is the maximum penalty, he would then not be eligible for community-based sentences, which by law, are only generally available for offences punishable with a maximum imprisonment term of not more than three years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The third case is the 23-year-old university student who committed voyeurism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offenders who commit such offences should not expect to be treated leniently.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Beyond these penalties, the criminal justice system also reflects the values of society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Such acts must be seen as penalising a gross violation of fundamental values in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The usual mitigating factors will have less force when viewed in this prism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The starting point should be the conduct should never have happened.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Offenders should expect to face the full force of the law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Society needs to play its part as well to unequivocally repudiate sexual and hurt offences as violations of fundamental values.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Collectively, with right laws and policies, and more importantly, with the right societal mindset in place, we can move towards being a society that fully lives up to our values.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I take the Minister back to the debate when the Criminal Law Reform Bill was tabled in Parliament in 2019.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These included road rage, secret society members, fighting, racial, religiously-aggravated VCH cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That question actually highlights one of the more involved discussions that MHA has been having, with me involved.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Voluntarily causing hurt, as Mr Singh would know, it can cover a broad ambit.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Let us leave out the sexual part of it – just two men.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You did not feel hurt, nothing, but he should not have pushed you.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the other end of the scale, could be a more serious assault which does not result in grievous hurt – because then, it would be voluntarily causing grievous hurt – but nevertheless, leaves you in a state of shock.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is quite clear the second category — I mean, we talk about Singapore being a safe society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need to know that if there is that kind of conduct, that will end up in court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you start taking every assault to court, I do not think we are doing justice as a society either.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because you will get into a detailed involved assessment of intent, cause.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the intent of your question then and now, Mr Singh, is that the criminal law is not the best solution for these cases.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It should be dealt with through other ways, without undermining the rule of law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There are some internal frameworks for the Police to try and assess that and deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If the Police try to deal every single case of police report on voluntarily causing hurt, it would be an impossible situation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I do not think we will be better off as a society either.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there is a framework to try and deal with this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, people who are not happy, there are other routes, as the Member knows as well; through a magistrate's route as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you want more details of how we work it, to the extent that it is possible to give it, because we do not want people gaming it either, I am happy to share the details.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I think we certainly welcome the new framework.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I have spoken on this on a number of occasions and I welcome the updates.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just one clarification I seek from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In the last two years, one of the questions that was raised is, quite a number of cases relate to those who have a position of trust with the victim.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just to rattle off some recent cases: teacher molests seven boys, former Secondary school teacher abuses 15-year-old students, Secondary school teacher molests boy in school lab, Primary school teacher molests 12-year-old boy and so on.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: You also have, recently: male nurse allegedly molests male patient, Statutory Board director outrages modesty of female subordinate, doctor at Mt E accused of molest against a female patient.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Many of these are in a position of trust.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean he reeled off a list of cases where people have abused that position of trust to molest or otherwise hurt someone close to them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Societal relationships, man's behaviour with man, these things happen everywhere.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not want people to go away thinking that, in some way, in Singapore, it is more extreme.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is much lower because, as I have said before – and I think Senior Minister Teo might have, too – in Singapore, a few things are quite certain.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When you have done wrong, you are likely to be investigated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the investigations do not usually take very long.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, if you are guilty, you are likely to be found guilty and you are likely to face the penalties because we start off from that framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Also, on the whole, we have a highly law-and-order-based society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we have managed to keep the criminal behaviour to a much smaller context than many other countries do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we start from a position which would be of some envy to most well-ordered societies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: With that, the specific question that Mr Yam has asked, these factors are already relevant, highly relevant, for sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is, of course, without considering, if you are a professional, the professional bodies will have something to say.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For doctors, the Medical Council will follow up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I agree with the Minister that we are starting from a position of strength.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My question is in relation to the handout provided.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: My question here is really that it is good that we protect our foreign domestic workers because they are in a position of vulnerability.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But I think that section 73 should be widened not just to include foreign domestic workers, but people who are in a position of vulnerability because of their employment.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And that can expand beyond the FDW matrix.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, if we are, indeed, wanting to protect the vulnerable, then would a reconsideration of section 73 and the widening of it be considered in this review?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the current position, we were quite deliberate that it should cover vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And in my speech now, as well as when I moved the amendments, the way we saw our society, what is happening, you have children who are vulnerable, you have domestic workers who are vulnerable and, in a fast-ageing society, you have senior citizens who are vulnerable, who are not able to take care of themselves, and you have intellectually-challenged people who are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have sought to define people in vulnerable categories; and offences against them, the penalties are much more severe.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we have already gone down that route and the definition is quite comprehensive in terms of starting with what we mean by "vulnerable".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, all those categories I have mentioned are considered vulnerable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We then added on another category that would not, in the usual sense, be considered vulnerable – girlfriends or people in an intimate partner relationship when they are subjected to violence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If you are in a marriage situation, the Women's Charter allows you to go and take an application, a Personal Protection Order (PPO).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if you are an unmarried partner, you cannot go and take a PPO under the Women's Charter because, by definition, it only applies to people who are married, spouses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I will be happy to ask my Ministry to relook at it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we were quite focused in the way our society was changing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Particularly, I was concerned about senior citizens who now are at homes, and elder abuse, and I felt that we ought to stiffen the law before it becomes prevalent.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have two clarifications for the Minister on what he said earlier regarding the policy that the AG in general will object to a rehabilitative sentence for certain kinds of offences.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, my first clarification on this is: is there going to be a change in the law to specifically provide that rehabilitative sentences will not be available to certain categories of offences?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second clarification is: I think it is important also for the Minister to confirm that these moves in no way undermine prosecutorial discretion which is provided for under the Constitution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: So, I would like him to confirm that, so that there is no misunderstanding on this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the second question whether this undermined prosecutorial discretion, absolutely not.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I mean, as I have mentioned in my Ministerial Statement, you will have cases where individuals – intellectually-challenged, did not know what they were doing was right or wrong or on the margin – these are not matters that we can set out in broad terms here in Parliament, and AGC will have to decide, case by case, and the Courts will have to decide case by case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But what is important is that Parliament understands and affirms, and the Executive, my Ministry, puts before Parliament the Government's policy and this Ministerial Statement sets out the Government's policy for Singaporeans, which we put before Parliament that we will take a no-nonsense approach to sexual and hurt offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is for the Government to set out that policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is for Parliament to put that policy in law where it is not already in law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I have said we will make amendments in three specific situations, and we set out what we believe should be the approach which is good for society as a whole.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that then has got to be the guidelines for AGC to apply in exercising their prosecutorial discretion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The discretion has got to have a framework to be applied; framework has got to be supplied by Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And for the Courts, with their judicial independence to apply, the Courts also need a framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, that is the context to the Statement.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I think his unequivocal Statement, in relation to the fact that qualifications of an offender would not matter in relation to sentencing, will go a long way to assuage members of the public that he were concerned about the sentences imposed on offenders that the hon Minister mentioned.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My clarification is on the Sentencing Advisory Council.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister mentioned that his Ministries will be looking at this.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The second clarification concerns the Attorney General's role.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister spoke about the case whereby the 22-year-old undergraduate strangled and I think injured his ex-girlfriend's eye as well.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I note that, in that case, actually, there were two offences that he committed.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Attorney General, or rather, the Public Prosecutor applied for the criminal trespass charge to be taken into consideration for purpose of sentencing and I also understand that there was no appeal arising from the sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that the hon Minister mentioned, in answer to the hon Member Ms Sylvia Lim, that it has been a practice of the AGC to object to rehabilitative and community sentences in relation to such offences, why then was there not an appeal?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And in relation to the offence that was taken into consideration, it was criminal trespass but, as I understand, the offence was that he broke into the house of the girlfriend, and the Penal Code has an aggravated form of offence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Housebreaking is an offence for which the offence is punishable by three years' sentence.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, may I understand what is the AGC policy in relation to such matters where there is hurt in the context of a relationship?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Precisely which offences would be covered, I do not want to prejudge that at this point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, specific to the facts of the 22-year-old undergraduate, under the criminal trespass charge that was taken into consideration, this goes directly into what Ms Sylvia Lim had asked.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is really not for me to second-guess and say, on specific cases, why the Attorney General's Chambers did or did not do something.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But let me recall or put across the facts as I remember them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was a case where, yes, there was a break-in but the ex-girlfriend then spent some time talking to the young man.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, in fact, took him – if I recall correctly – to a part of the house.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It may well be, if I were the prosecutor, I would look at it and I will say that that is not going to be an easy case, because, yes, there was initial trespass but was there subsequent consent?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, one has got to look at the facts carefully.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There can be a variety of reasons why charges are taken into consideration.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, it was dealt with in accordance with the law at that point in time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, this would have been treated like an intimate partner violence case, where the penalty would be higher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I cannot be dealing with every specific discretion that AGC exercises.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first, from a victim-centric point of view.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Second, Sir, the trauma on victims can be irreversible.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But I have spoken in this House about going beyond second chances and I have worked with young offenders and families with people incarcerated.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is very evident from heated discussions online that there is significant public interest in this space.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We can express our views set out in the Parliament through legislation – tough laws – but let us not walk out of this Chamber with the belief that the laws alone or even the enforcement of them is going to prevent all offences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The one thing I have learned in 30 years in the law, in one way or another, is that the laws are there, the majority of the people do not need laws to keep them straight and a small minority who will be tempted, many of them will not be tempted as long as they know that the laws are tough and there will be enforcement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But there will always be, regardless of what steps you put in to prevent fraud, what steps you put in to prevent criminal action, there will always be a group that breaks the laws.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Having the laws is important for the bulk of society but let us be clear – there will be people who will break them and we will have to deal with it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether it is laws against sexual offences or laws against fraud or laws against speeding; any of which.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we think that that might help reduce the victim's trauma from having to recount again in court the ordeal the person went through.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are trying to reduce the number of times a person has got to talk about the ordeal that he or she went through; usually a "she".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But when we speak about all of this, do not forget the presumption of innocence and the accused's right to a fair trial and have the allegations tested in court.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, Ms Nadia Ahman Samdin also asked about the role of media and members of the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In order to have meaningful discourse, you need a better understanding.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: To raise the level of understanding, we are, for example, publishing the guide on sentencing that I spoke about in my Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are also talking about the Sentencing Advisory Panel issuing guidelines.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But, of course, I think we must be realistic.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Not every member is going to check out the MHA website on guidelines and read them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think a few days ago I recall Mr Pritam Singh saying that he did not realise that I had made nine speeches.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am realistic about how many people read my speeches and visit the MHA website.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But we will put it out and we will try and get people to understand.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, lawyers will be better informed as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The media, I think they play a very important role, in helping the public get a fuller and better understanding of the process and what is the framework.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But I think one point to which I do not really have a solution is that individual cases, partially reported, without the full facts, tend to invoke a lot of passion, excite a lot of passion, and then people form views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to be careful about the cases being trialed in the court of public opinion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Or there being decisions which are pushed upon by the public with not a full understanding either of the law or the facts.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because not the full facts are out in the media most of the time.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have to allow judges to carry on and do their jobs.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But public opinion is important and for the Parliament to be aware of the public sense of right and wrong is also important because that allows us to calibrate and make sure our laws accurately reflect where the balance ought to lie.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Now, we ought to decide that – in the best interests of the public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But public viewpoints and public opinions are relevant in coming to that assessment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Nadia Ahman Samdin also asked about the balance between deterrence and rehabilitation in sentencing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Most of my speech – quite a lot of my speech – was targeted at dealing with that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Again, it is for the Parliament to decide, depending on the offence, what the balance ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is why in my Ministerial Statement I spoke about adult offenders being treated more severely.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You would treat a 15-year-old differently from a 25-year-old or a 23-year-old.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We need to look at the degree of active consideration of what the person was going to do, the culpability, the seriousness of the offence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For younger offenders, the general approach – the dominant factor – ought to be rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Because they do not have the full maturity of adults and they are still in their formative years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But other sentencing principles, like deterrence and proportionate punishment, may take precedence over rehabilitation, even for younger offenders, where the offence is serious, the harm caused is severe, the offender in our assessment is hardened or recalcitrant, or the conditions that make rehabilitation options viable do not exist.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As an advocate to end domestic violence, I really appreciate the statements made.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One on the guidelines themselves, second on the composition of this advisory panel.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the guidelines, I understand that the guidelines are non-binding but highly persuasive.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, they amended the Evidence Act to make those guidelines binding upon the courts but the courts can depart from them if it is in the course of justice to do so.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But if I may offer another alternative position used in the Victorian courts, where the panel themselves can be invited by the court of appeal to provide some views before the sentencing of a particular case.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I say this so that we do not shut out any possibility or flexibility to cater to evolving societal needs and specific individual cases.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the second part, the composition of the panel, I ask the Ministry to consider a diversity, both in terms of gender and also expertise.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, it is about 60% women but also entirely made up of legal professionals and judiciary.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But in Victoria, it is about 50% women but comprising victims, crime support advocacy groups and also criminal justice professionals.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Perhaps the Minister can see whether the Ministry can consider such diversity in the panel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First off, it would look a little odd that judges appear before judges to give their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the composition that we are thinking of will have judges, practitioners, lawyers certainly, appointed by the Law Minister.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The way we are thinking of, MinLaw might appoint two.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Who those two persons will be, we will decide on whether it needs to be from the Bar or from other places.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be widely known across the legal and judicial circles.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think that it helps us put up a framework beyond the legislation.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether you need to go further, we can look at things as they evolve, but we also need to be careful how we structure it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am a believer that you appoint the appropriate persons to the right job.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The guidelines from the panel must carry weight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must have gravitas for judges to take it seriously.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That does not mean that you cannot take in the viewpoints of a variety of people interested in this matter.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: NGOs will have interest, others would have an interest, people who want specific laws or specific types of penalties to be changed will have an interest.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And you must appoint a panel that is open to hearing all these viewpoints.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But the panel must have the expertise to make an assessment based on the law and what makes sense, and put it across.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Open-minded, but an open mind is not an empty mind.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must also not absorb whatever nonsense that comes up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It must be able to assess what makes sense, what does not make sense, make an assessment, give guidelines that would carry authority and respect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They will all be welcome to give their views.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The primary goal must be a sentencing body that would carry respect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In terms of gender diversity, I do not think Mr Zhulkanain or Members need to worry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is something that my Ministry will keep front and centre, and even if we did not, I think more than half the profession are women anyway.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you will expect that to be reflected in the panel.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But I do have a clarification though, on the Sentencing Advisory Panel.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But perhaps can I ask Ms Poa, in principle, does she support the setting up of a Sentencing Advisory Panel?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, we may be able to discuss further.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I am afraid that I will not be able to answer that question because I need clarifications on how this sentencing panel will influence the Judiciary.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: My concern is actually about whether it would compromise their independence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Ms Poa understands what I am asking, but she does not want to answer.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Why should it compromise the independence of theJudiciary?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First of all, I said more than half the members would be from the Judiciary.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, the purpose is guidelines for the future without referring to any specific case.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Just like here, we are discussing what the laws ought to be.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we compromise the independence of the Judiciary by doing so?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Do we compromise the independence of the Judiciary when we set out in the law, what the punishments ought to be?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Those decisions are made, that is a framework in which the laws are applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The guidelines are guidelines which will flesh out a little bit more.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And it is for the Courts and the judges in the individual cases to decide whether the guidelines need to be departed from or need to be applied.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How do the giving of these guidelines, how do the guidelines that the Courts have internally, how does any of this compromise the independence of the Judiciary?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On Ms Poa's reckoning, the judiciaries in Australia and UK are no longer independent.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: The range of sentencing will be actually specified in the law.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: And within that, the Courts then mete out individual sentences for each case.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: But so how does this Sentencing Advisory Panel add on to what is in the law?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa
text: I need further clarification on how it will work.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think I have tried to explain this a number of times.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The law cannot, if you look at the legal provisions, go into much more detail than that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Sometimes, you can have illustrations, you can have some examples.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Generally, we think the range of sentences, our view is that it should be between this and this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is bringing together a combined wisdom to set out a framework for how cases can be dealt with and it is aid for the individual judges faced with individual cases and applying the law and the guidelines to the specific facts to see whether the facts come within, should it fall within this range or there are facts which take it out.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I said, on the reasoning of Ms Poa, a number of judiciaries around the world would not be considered independent.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I fully support the measures and the framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I just want to make a point on behalf of workers, particularly, in four sectors: healthcare workers, transport workers, private security workers, as well as cleaning sector workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am fully aware that section 6 of the Prevention of Harassment Act does extend to Public Service workers and we have enhanced that.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Whether Minister can consider in view of the vulnerability or should I say in a sense that they are essential workers, consider covering them within the ambit of this framework.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Perhaps consider them as in a position where we need better protection for them and in more deterrent sentences.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think we need to be careful about using the tag of vulnerability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Certain categories of workers that you have mentioned perform essential services, they are front facing, they face people and we need to help them because they are more often abused.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you got to find the right rubric.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The right rubric is therefore not to extend the categories of vulnerable victims.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the right rubric is to say these people face bigger risks and can we identify them or people who fall in those categories for some additional protection?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, public sector workers, essential workers, these are all defined and may help them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I think upon your advocacy, we have also extended greater protection to other categories of workers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is possible to work the law towards covering different categories, but you must use the right framework.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, it did not mention MinLaw's effort to protect victims of workplace sexual harassment, which is also very serious.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, my question is, has the Government done any victimisation surveys of its own to uncover the extent of workplace sexual harassment in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And secondly, are there plans to table any legislation to oblige employers to prevent and address workplace sexual harassment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I understand that TAFEP has issued a tripartite advisory on managing workplace harassment and that is quite comprehensive.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: So, would it be better to give the TAFEP advisory more teeth?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I understand Mr Giam's question, for harassment, there is a continuum.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There is harassment which does not cross the threshold of criminality and then there is a harassment that does cross that threshold.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Once it crosses the threshold, that is what I have been talking about, amongst other things.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure Mr Giam was in Parliament then, but when POHA was amended, it specifically allows individuals who feel harassed to take steps and to prevent the harassment, because, as I said, not all harassment amounts to criminal conduct.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We drew a line ahead of whatever is criminal and said individuals, you can go and get remedies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, there are these steps that have already been taken.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whatever the law can do, we have done.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, from the legal perspective, we have empowered the individual, we have tightened up the criminal law.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The laws stand there, first, to give aid and succour to individuals; and second, to protect them through the criminal process against the offender.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think the essence of Mr Giam's question really is, beyond the legal framework, can more things be done from the perspective of employers and workplace safety.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And that is a question I would invite him to file with MOM.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I think it is really important and I am grateful for the Government in taking a strong stand against the sexual offences and hurt to better protect women and girls.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have a question and I will take the opportunity to ask.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It is not so much related to this particular sentencing framework.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But to address the trend whether the norm in society where women are subject to sexual objectification, often in the media.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I have come across residents' parents who grapple with their young children being exposed or even exchanging sexual content over the phone and so on with their peers – as young as the Primary school age.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: So, I think that is a very alarming phenomenon.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And also, I would like to express my gratitude for the fact that sexual communications are now a category of offences to avoid sexual grooming of persons from a young age.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But I think the general societal exposure to sexual content, victimising or objectifying women, might be something that we want to address on a broader scale.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The other question is a much broader one – sexual objectification.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is beyond the remit of Home Affairs and Law because we deal with crime and punishment.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But it is precisely the topic that is front and centre for the women's conversation, which has been kicked off in September of last year.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I spoke about it when I started off my Ministerial Statement.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: These cases where the boys going to girls' toilets in universities and take a video, and they think of it as a prank or something that is cool to do.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And if we approach it simply from a criminal law perspective, yes, we will keep putting these boys into prison.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But while we have to take a tough approach, what is really needed is a new approach and new way, a change of mindset.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Which is why last year, when we kicked off this entire process of having conversations on women's development, I spoke about us having to affirm the status of women, the inviolability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And every boy and girl has got to grow up learning that respect for women is a non-negotiable point.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And, therefore, it is not cool to go and do this.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a serious violation of a fundamental value.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That has got to pervade across all sectors, including the media.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Against that are very powerful countervailing forces – the power of money and what sells.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What makes a film more watchable, what makes a TV show successful?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In a context where people will do everything possible to push their products, including objectifying women in the process, if they can sell more cars or whatever.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But how should we approach it as a society?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is a value system and it is going to require a mindset change, it is going to require education.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The answer does not lie with the law alone.
